design_detail: Invited narrative review in Current Opinion in Hematology (5 pages, 44 references) by two emergency physicians and medical toxicologists at the Rocky Mountain Poison and Drug Center, Denver, on the medical consequences of levamisole in illicit cocaine: agranulocytosis, cutaneous vasculopathy, leukoencephalopathy, other effects, and laboratory testing. There is no search strategy, no selection criteria and no appraisal of the cited studies. The human evidence cited is case reports and case series, two urine-prevalence studies, and analyses of seized drugs.
can_establish: What the case literature up to 2011 described for agranulocytosis and skin vasculopathy in people who had used levamisole-contaminated cocaine (clinical picture, timing of neutrophil recovery, autoantibodies, histology), what the authors advised for hospital work-up, and the detection windows they give for levamisole in blood and urine.
cannot_establish: How often people exposed to levamisole through cocaine develop any of these conditions (no incidence among exposed people is given anywhere); that levamisole rather than cocaine itself causes a given case (attribution in the cited reports rests mostly on cocaine use and the known effects of medical levamisole, with laboratory confirmation of levamisole in a minority); that leukoencephalopathy occurs through cocaine (the review says no such case had been reported); or how well any treatment works (no controlled data).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Evidence cited: case reports and series of agranulocytosis and vasculopathy (refs 13, 14, 18–20, 24–44), two 2011 urine studies from Denver and San Francisco (refs 11, 12), US seizure data and a Luxembourg analysis of seized cocaine (refs 9, 10), and older literature on medical use of levamisole.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No search or selection criteria stated; the stated aim is to outline findings from the preceding year (p. 27).
sample.selection_effects: Author-selected literature, mostly case reports, which favour severe, unusual or well-documented cases. Three cited papers (refs 11, 18, 31) and both figures come from the first author's own work. No study with a denominator of exposed people is cited for any complication.

exposure.measurement: As summarized: exposure to levamisole is inferred from cocaine use (history, or benzoylecgonine in urine), with levamisole itself detected in some cases; the first case report with laboratory confirmation of levamisole appeared in early 2010 (ref. 18, p. 28).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Only the adulterant content of seized cocaine is reported: levamisole first detected by the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) in 2003; 30% of cocaine exhibits adulterated by 2008; 73.2% of cocaine analysed by the DEA containing levamisole in January 2010; levamisole at 1.5–4.1% in Luxembourg seizures (p. 28). Cases followed smoking, injection and nasal use; most agranulocytosis cases followed smoking, without a clear difference in risk by route (p. 28).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; the review names lidocaine-like local anaesthetics and diltiazem as other cutting agents in cocaine (p. 28).

comparison.controls: None. The only comparisons offered are the background incidence of agranulocytosis in the general population, about 5 cases per million per year (ref. 6, p. 28), and the 0.4–20% of medically treated patients who formed antineutrophil antibodies (p. 27).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; the review notes that a genetic predisposition (HLA-B27, HLA class 1) reported for medical levamisole had not been studied in people exposed through cocaine (p. 29).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (review). Testing described: gas chromatography–mass spectrometry for levamisole in urine and plasma, available at public-health, reference and crime laboratories (p. 30).
outcomes.operationalization: Agranulocytosis, neutropenia, cutaneous vasculopathy and leukoencephalopathy as described in the cited cases; no case definitions are given.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Second-hand figures: background agranulocytosis incidence about 5 per million per year (p. 28); antineutrophil antibodies in 0.4–20% of medically treated patients (p. 27); levamisole in 78% (Denver) and 88% (San Francisco) of urine samples positive for cocaine metabolites (p. 28); about half of the patients in the Alberta–British Columbia series had more than one episode of agranulocytosis with renewed cocaine use (p. 28); spontaneous neutrophil recovery 5–10 days after exposure ends, against recovery within 2–3 days of GCSF in most case reports (p. 29); neutropenia in about half of vasculopathy cases (p. 30); levamisole plasma half-life about 5.6 hours, and urine positive for about 2–3 days (p. 30).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not applicable as such; several figures carry no citation (the January 2010 DEA figure, the SAMHSA estimate, the 5.6-hour half-life), and the 2008 figure is cited to a source that cannot contain it (reporting issues).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The review describes case reports and small series of agranulocytosis and skin vasculopathy in people who had used cocaine, frequent detection of levamisole in seized cocaine and in the urine of patients testing positive for cocaine in two cities, spontaneous neutrophil recovery within about 5–10 days of stopping exposure, no treatment trials, and no reported case of leukoencephalopathy acquired through cocaine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary says more than three fourths of people who use cocaine in the US are exposed to levamisole and that a "significant minority" will develop neutropenia, vasculopathy and/or leukoencephalopathy (p. 27). Gaps: (1) the three-fourths figure rests on urine samples from two hospital populations (78% and 88%) and on seizure data (73.2%, which is below three fourths) (p. 28); (2) no incidence among exposed people is cited, so the significant minority has no number behind it; (3) the body states that no case of leukoencephalopathy through cocaine had been reported (p. 30), yet the Purpose (levamisole known to cause neurologic complications), the Summary and the Conclusion list it among the consequences (pp. 27, 30); (4) whether levamisole or cocaine causes the cases is not discussed, although most cited cases were not laboratory-confirmed. The Key Points and Conclusion (ask patients about cocaine, defer extensive work-up while waiting for spontaneous recovery) are the authors' clinical opinion for hospital care.

timeline.event: First reports of agranulocytosis after levamisole-contaminated cocaine in Alberta, British Columbia, New Mexico, Washington, Arizona and Colorado (refs 13, 14, as cited p. 28)
First case report of agranulocytosis with laboratory confirmation of levamisole (Buchanan et al., J Med Toxicol; ref. 18)
Urine studies in Denver and San Francisco: levamisole in 78% and 88% of samples positive for cocaine metabolites (refs 11, 12, as cited p. 28)
Pathology review of levamisole-induced vasculitis for pathologists

replication.where_it_stands: A narrative summary of the early case literature. On how often complications occur among exposed people it offers nothing; causal attribution rests on the pattern of cases and on the known effects of medical levamisole. Claims should cite the primary series (and later systematic work, if found) with their case definitions and testing, using this review only for the clinical description and the testing windows.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state that there are no conflicts of interest (p. 30).
funding.affiliations_note: Rocky Mountain Poison and Drug Center, Denver Health and Hospital Authority, and University of Colorado School of Medicine (p. 27). The first author's own case reports and urine-prevalence study are among the main sources (refs 11, 18, 31).

what_would_settle_it: A population-based case–control or cohort study of people who use cocaine, with levamisole measured in cases and comparison participants alike, to estimate how often agranulocytosis and vasculopathy occur per exposed person and whether levamisole explains them beyond cocaine itself.

domains.note: Case reports and series are summarized without appraising how cases were identified or whether levamisole was confirmed.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of the first author's papers (refs 11, 18, 31) and both figures; otherwise the case literature is cited widely.

The idea that levamisole makes cocaine more reinforcing is labelled as theory (p. 28), but the Summary and Conclusion present leukoencephalopathy through cocaine as an established consequence although no case had been reported (pp. 27, 30).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how often and how surely levamisole harms people exposed through cocaine (exposed people without complications, and cocaine itself as an alternative cause, are under-represented)
domains.note: Exposure is described as near-universal and complications as affecting a significant minority without any incidence figure, and the vascular effects of cocaine itself are not weighed as an alternative explanation.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist gives high concern overall, driven by the absence of a systematic search or appraisal and by a one-sided framing of frequency. The review is a fair clinical description of the case literature to 2011 and cites its sources. Claims may cite it for the clinical picture, the timing of neutrophil recovery reported in cases, the testing windows, and the seizure and urine prevalence figures (second-hand, with their sources); never for how often complications occur, and not for leukoencephalopathy acquired through cocaine.

key_findings.finding: Prevalence of levamisole cited: first detected by the DEA in cocaine seized in 2003; 30% of cocaine exhibits adulterated by 2008; 73.2% of cocaine analysed by the DEA in January 2010 contained levamisole; in Luxembourg seizures levamisole was the commonest adulterant, at 1.5–4.1%; in 2011, levamisole was found in 78% (Denver) and 88% (San Francisco) of urine samples positive for cocaine metabolites.
key_findings.note: The 2008 figure is cited to ref. 3, a 1999 report on children treated with levamisole, which cannot be its source; the January 2010 figure has no citation.

key_findings.finding: Agranulocytosis after levamisole-contaminated cocaine was first reported in 2009 (Alberta, British Columbia, New Mexico, Washington, Arizona, Colorado); the first case with laboratory confirmation of levamisole was published in early 2010. Most cases followed smoking, without a clear difference in risk by route; about half of the patients in one series had repeat episodes with renewed cocaine use.

Mechanism as summarized: levamisole is thought to act as a hapten, leading to antibodies against neutrophils; 0.4–20% of patients treated medically formed such antibodies; ANCA are also commonly detected; the bone marrow is typically hypercellular with relative myeloid hypoplasia, with or without megakaryocyte hyperplasia.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 4th paragraph (pp. 27–28); Neutropenia and Agranulocytosis, 1st paragraph (pp. 28–29); Figure 1 (p. 29)

key_findings.finding: Treatment of agranulocytosis: no controlled trials; most case reports describe neutrophil recovery within 2–3 days of GCSF, but spontaneous recovery 5–10 days after exposure ends is also described, so the added benefit of GCSF in patients without active infection is unclear; the authors suggest deferring marrow biopsy in neutropenic patients with a clear history of cocaine exposure unless counts fail to recover in the expected time.

Cutaneous vasculopathy, described from a large number of anecdotal reports since 2009 (refs 24–44): purpuric plaques in a retiform or stellate pattern, bullae, necrosis, ulcers; typical sites ears, cheeks, nose and extremities; women predominate among cases although cocaine use is more common in men; diffuse autoantibodies (antineutrophil, c- and p-ANCA, anticardiolipin, anti-dsDNA, antiphospholipid); small-vessel vasculitis, thrombotic vasculopathy or both on histology; neutropenia in about half of cases.
key_findings.locator: Cutaneous Vasculopathy, 1st paragraph (begins p. 29, ends p. 30)

key_findings.finding: Lesions usually resolve within a few weeks of stopping cocaine; other treatments used (corticosteroids, colchicine, phentolamine, anticoagulation, skin grafting) lack systematically collected data.

Leukoencephalopathy has been associated with medical levamisole; no case acquired through cocaine had been reported at the time, though the authors mention one probable case at their institution without details; no data support or refute any treatment.

Testing: levamisole can be detected by GC-MS in urine and plasma; its plasma half-life is about 5.6 hours (estimated population mean), so serum is likely negative when the last exposure was more than 24 hours earlier; urine stays positive about as long as benzoylecgonine, roughly 2–3 days in most patients. The authors consider specific testing unnecessary in many cases.
key_findings.note: No source is cited for the 5.6-hour figure; refs 11 and 12 are cited for the urine window.

key_findings.finding: Background incidence of agranulocytosis in the general population: about 5 cases per million per year (ref. 6).
No incidence of any complication among people exposed to levamisole through cocaine is given anywhere in the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Summary says a significant minority of exposed people will develop leukoencephalopathy, and the Purpose that levamisole is known to cause neurologic complications (p. 27), but the body states that no case acquired through cocaine had been reported (p. 30).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the body: no case reported at the time.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2008 figure (30% of cocaine exhibits adulterated) is cited to ref. 3, a 1999 report on children treated with levamisole; the January 2010 DEA figure (73.2%), the SAMHSA estimate of 5.9 million people aged 12 and over using cocaine in 2002–2003 (measure not stated) and the 5.6-hour half-life carry no citation.
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures cannot be traced through the review; cite primary sources.

reporting_issues.issue: More than three fourths exposed (Summary, p. 27) is not supported by the figures cited for it: 73.2% of seized cocaine, and 78% and 88% of urine samples in two hospital populations (p. 28).
reporting_issues.consequence: Generalizes from two urban hospital samples to all people who use cocaine in the US.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 31 (the first author's report of ear vasculitis) is given as J Med Toxicol 2011;29:299–303, while ref. 18 in the same list gives J Med Toxicol 2010;6:160–164; the project's cocaine reading list records this report as Buchanan et al. 2010.
reporting_issues.consequence: Check the citation details before linking ref. 31 to a project record.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Current Opinion in Hematology 19(1), pp. 27–31 (all pages read on 150-dpi renderings; Figures 1–2 are images, described from their legends; no supplement).
